{{short description|Graph edge coloring with a limited number of allowed colors}}
[[File:List-edge coloring (cb).svg|thumb|270px|This assignment of lists, each with length {{mvar|k}} = 3, makes it so that no matter which colors are chosen from each list for the edge's color, the graph cannot be [[edge coloring|properly colored]]. The graph is therefore ''not'' '''3-edge-choosable''', and has a '''list chromatic index''' of at least 4 (in this case, it is 4).]]
{{unsolved|mathematics|For every graph, is the list chromatic index equal to the chromatic index?}}

In [[graph theory]], '''list edge-coloring''' is a type of [[graph coloring]] that combines [[list coloring]] and [[edge coloring]].
An instance of a list edge-coloring problem consists of a graph together with a list of allowed colors for each edge. A list edge-coloring is a choice of a color for each edge, from its list of allowed colors; a coloring is proper if no two adjacent edges receive the same color.

A graph {{mvar|G}} is '''{{mvar|k}}-edge-choosable''' if every instance of list edge-coloring that has {{mvar|G}} as its underlying graph and that provides at least {{mvar|k}} allowed colors for each edge of {{mvar|G}} has a proper coloring. In other words, when the list for each edge has length {{mvar|k}}, no matter which colors are put in each list, a color can be selected from each list so that {{mvar|G}} is properly colored.
The '''edge choosability''', or ''list edge colorability'', ''list edge chromatic number'', or ''list chromatic index'', {{math|ch'(''G'')}} of graph {{mvar|G}} is the least number {{mvar|k}} such that {{mvar|G}} is {{mvar|k}}-edge-choosable. It is conjectured that it always equals the [[chromatic index]].

==Properties==
Here {{math|''χ''{{prime}}(''G'')}} is the [[Edge coloring|chromatic index]] of {{mvar|G}}; and {{mvar|K{{sub|n,n}}}}, the [[complete bipartite graph]] with equal [[Glossary of graph theory|partite sets]].

Some properties of {{math|ch'(''G'')}}:
# <math>\operatorname{ch}'(G) < 2 \chi'(G).</math>
# <math>\operatorname{ch}'(K_{n,n}) = n.</math>  This is the [[Dinitz theorem]], proven by {{harvtxt|Galvin|1995}}.
# <math>\operatorname{ch}'(G) < (1 + o(1)) \chi'(G),</math> i.e. the list chromatic index and the chromatic index agree asymptotically {{harv|Kahn|2000}}.
# For bipartite graphs, <math>ch'(G)=\chi'(G)</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Galvin |first=Fred |date=June 28, 1994 |title=The List Chromatic Index of a Bipartite Multigraph |url=https://kostochk.web.illinois.edu/math581/galvin.pdf |journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory Series B |volume=63 |pages=153-158}}</ref> For every simple [[bipartite graph]], <math>ch'(G)=\Delta</math>.<ref name="BondyMurty">{{cite book |last1=Bondy |first1=J. A. |last2=Murty |first2=U. S. R. |title=Graph theory |date=2008 |publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-1-84628-969-9 |pages=466-469}}</ref>

==List coloring conjecture==
The most famous open problem about list edge-coloring is probably the ''list coloring conjecture''.

<math display=block>\operatorname{ch}'(G) = \chi'(G).</math>

This conjecture has a fuzzy origin; {{harvtxt|Jensen|Toft|1995}} overview its history. The Dinitz conjecture, proven by {{harvtxt|Galvin|1995}}, is the special case of the list coloring conjecture for the [[complete bipartite graph]]s {{mvar|K<sub>n,n</sub>}}.
